title: Drug Classes in Pharmacology
subject: Pharmacology
summary: A clinician‑oriented overview of major drug classes, their mechanisms, typical indications in low‑resource settings and key considerations for safe prescribing.

sections.p: Drug classes group medicines by shared mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics or therapeutic use. Recognising the class guides choice, predicts side‑effects and avoids harmful interactions.
b: Class = mechanism‑based grouping (e.g., β‑blockers block β‑adrenergic receptors).
Clinicians think “what is the target?” before picking a specific agent.

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the most common conditions dictate which drug classes you will use daily.
b: Infectious diseases – malaria, TB, HIV, bacterial sepsis → antimalarials, anti‑TB, antiretrovirals, antibiotics.
Cardiovascular emergencies – hypertension, heart failure, arrhythmia → antihypertensives, diuretics, anti‑arrhythmics.
Pain and inflammation – trauma, post‑surgical pain, osteoarthritis → NSAIDs, opioids, steroids.

sections.p: Patients arrive with a syndrome; the drug class needed is inferred from the syndrome’s pathophysiology.
b: Fever + positive malaria smear → antimalarial class (e.g., artemisinin‑based).
Cough, weight loss, night sweats, sputum + GeneXpert positive → anti‑TB class (rifampicin‑based).
Acute chest pain, ST‑elevation → antiplatelet + anticoagulant class.

sections.p: Tests are ordered to confirm the underlying disease and to guide drug‑class selection.

t.b: Confirms malaria infection → need for antimalarial class; if negative, consider other causes.
Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance → determines anti‑TB regimen.
Establishes HIV status → initiates antiretroviral therapy class.
Assesses renal function before using renally cleared classes (e.g., aminoglycosides).
Guides choice of antihypertensive class (ACE‑I, calcium‑channel blocker, β‑blocker).

sections.p: Select the appropriate drug class, then individual agents, considering efficacy, safety, availability and interactions.
b: Antimalarials – artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT) because of rapid parasite clearance and low resistance.
Anti‑TB – rifampicin‑based regimen; rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, so avoid concurrent protease‑inhibitors.
Antiretrovirals – NNRTI‑based first line (efavirenz) in most East African protocols; avoid nevirapine in women with high CD4 due to hepatotoxicity.
Antibiotics – β‑lactam class for common Gram‑positive infections; reserve fluoroquinolones for resistant cases because of tendon toxicity.
NSAIDs – non‑selective COX inhibitors for mild‑moderate pain; avoid in patients with active peptic ulcer disease or severe renal impairment.
Opioids – weak opioid class (codeine) for moderate pain; strong opioid class (morphine) for severe pain, monitor for respiratory depression.

sections.p: Recognise adverse effects that require urgent action.
b: Stevens‑Johnson syndrome with sulfonamide antibiotics – stop class immediately.
Severe hepatotoxicity with isoniazid or NNRTIs – discontinue and refer.
Acute kidney injury after aminoglycoside use – stop class, hydrate, monitor creatinine.

sections.p: After initiating a class, arrange monitoring appropriate to its toxicity profile and reinforce preventive measures.
b: Liver function tests every 2–3 months for anti‑TB and NNRTI classes.
Blood pressure review after starting antihypertensive class.
Adherence counseling for ART class to prevent resistance.

sections.p: Drug classes can be mistaken for each other because of overlapping indications.
b: β‑blockers vs. calcium‑channel blockers – both lower BP but differ in effect on heart rate and asthma risk.
NSAIDs vs. COX‑2 selective inhibitors – similar analgesia, but COX‑2 spare GI mucosa.

sections.p: Laboratory or clinical findings may not reflect the true pharmacologic effect in low‑resource settings.
b: Normal creatinine in dehydration may mask early nephrotoxicity of aminoglycosides.
Negative malaria rapid test does not exclude low‑parasitaemia; consider microscopy if suspicion remains.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) after any drug class
Acute liver failure signs (jaundice, encephalopathy) while on hepatotoxic class
Sudden loss of consciousness after opioid class initiation

faq.q: Why learn drug classes instead of memorising individual drugs?
faq.a: Classes reveal the underlying mechanism, predict side‑effects and let you choose alternatives when a specific drug is unavailable.

faq.q: What if the recommended drug from a class is out of stock?
faq.a: Select another agent within the same class that is available; if none exist, move to the next class with a similar mechanism.

faq.q: How do I avoid dangerous drug interactions in a busy ward?
faq.a: Know the key enzyme inducers/inhibitors of each class (e.g., rifampicin induces CYP450) and check the patient’s current regimen before prescribing.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with new cough; GeneXpert shows rifampicin‑resistant TB – which drug class should be added and why? — Use a fluoroquinolone‑based class; avoid rifampicin due to resistance.
A patient on ART (NNRTI class) develops jaundice – what is the next step? — Stop NNRTI class, assess liver function, switch to integrase inhibitor class if available.
You have a malaria‑positive child but no ACT tablets; which alternative class can you use safely? — Use quinine class with appropriate dosing; explain why ACT is preferred but not available.
A hypertensive patient with asthma needs BP control – which antihypertensive class is contraindicated and why? — β‑blocker class is avoided because it can precipitate bronchospasm.

A postoperative patient on opioid analgesia becomes drowsy and hypoxic – which class‑related complication should you suspect? — Opioid class respiratory depression; stop opioid and provide airway support.

You need to start anti‑TB therapy but the patient has baseline ALT > 3 × ULN – how does this affect your choice of drug class? — Delay hepatotoxic class (isoniazid, pyrazinamide) and monitor; consider using a regimen with fewer liver‑toxic agents.

A child with severe bacterial infection is given a β‑lactam class antibiotic but develops a rash and fever – what is the likely diagnosis and next step? — Likely drug‑induced hypersensitivity; stop β‑lactam class and switch to a non‑β‑lactam class.

During a malaria outbreak, a patient refuses blood tests; which drug class can you safely give empirically? — ACT class can be given based on clinical diagnosis when testing unavailable, with counseling on side‑effects.
